### Prerequisites

This text has an application to practice, in a single place, the trigonometric functions and the relationships we derived from the circle. Before using it, we recommend studying the sine and cosine functions (<htcite0>; <htcite1>) and how we walked on the circle to discover their relationship (<htcite2>).

### Introduction

When we studied the trigonometric functions, we learned that each one relates an angle theta (θ) to one leg of the right triangle: the sine relates it to the opposite leg, and the cosine to the adjacent leg (<htcite0>; <htcite1>). When we walked on the circle, we also learned that the sum of the squares of these two functions is always equal to the square of the radius, which for the unit circle is 1 (<htcite2>):

cos2(θ)+sin2(θ)=1

Formula 1: Fundamental trigonometric identity.

In the previous texts, each relationship was practiced with its own application. Here, instead, we bring everything together: you can choose between the trigonometric functions and the trigonometric relationships, and then iterate with the app, moving the angle theta (θ) and observing how the triangle inside the circle changes together with the position of the point on the function chart.

### Practice

To better understand the connection between the triangle, the circle and the functions, we suggest that you move the angle theta (θ) in the following order:

As we can see, the triangle inside the circle and the chart always walk together: when the angle theta (θ) changes, the value of the chosen function changes, and the point in the chart moves along the first quadrant. Whatever mode you choose — a single function or a relationship — the sum of the squares of the sine and the cosine always remains 1 in the unit circle.

### Conclusion

In this text, we practiced the trigonometric functions and the trigonometric relationships in a single application. By selecting between functions and relationships and moving the angle theta (θ), we saw how the right triangle inside the circle is connected to the value of the functions and to the position of the point on the function chart in the first quadrant.
